population_detail: infants <27 completed gestational weeks, born 2004-2007 (EXPRESS study), Sweden
intervention: n/a (observational exposure: duration of hyperglycaemia >8 mmol/L)
outcomes_measured: WISC-IV FSIQ; MABC-2 total score at 6.5 years; insulin treatment as separate exposure
primary_result: each day of hyperglycaemia >8 mmol/L associated with lower FSIQ and MABC-2 scores; insulin treatment not associated with outcomes
effect_size: FSIQ -0.33 points/day; MABC-2 -0.55 points/day (continuous); MABC-2 adjusted mean difference -4.90 for >=3 consecutive days >8mmol/L
p_value: not reported as single p-value (regression coefficients with CIs)
secondary_results: insulin treatment showed no association (positive or negative) with any outcome measure - reported as null
ascertainment_method: prospectively and retrospectively collected national cohort data; WISC-IV and MABC-2 administered at 6.5 years
rob_tool: not applied (observational cohort; no formal RoB tool reported in abstract)
rob_overall: moderate (observational, national cohort, but exposure duration measured prospectively; residual confounding by illness severity plausible)
directness: DIRECT - extremely preterm (<27 weeks) - the most directly relevant hyperglycaemia population for a Level 3 NICU
grade_reason: indirectness low (matches target population exactly) but imprecision (wide CIs, e.g. FSIQ 0.03-0.62) and observational design (confounding by indication/illness severity not excluded)
key_limitation: key primary trace-back target for the Lagace/Tam U-shaped dysglycaemia claim in extremely preterm infants; insulin-treatment null is as prominent as the hyperglycaemia-duration positive finding
notes: Central extremely-preterm-specific evidence for this domain; duration/dose-response (not simple threshold breach) is the operative exposure metric
glucose_threshold_used: >8 mmol/L (144 mg/dL) as exposure threshold; U-shape review threshold >150-180mg/dL (8.3-10.0mmol/L) referenced separately
glucose_measurement_method: not specified in abstract (national cohort data collection)

population_detail: GA<32 weeks or BW<1500g, survived to 24 months
intervention: PN-related hyperglycaemia (glucose >180 mg/dL) in first week of life
outcomes_measured: Bayley-III cognitive and motor delay at 24 months corrected age
primary_result: hyperglycaemia associated with higher rates of cognitive and motor delay; motor delay remained significant after adjustment
effect_size: cognitive delay 44% vs 22%; motor delay 38% vs 8%
secondary_results: hyperglycaemia remained an independent risk factor for motor delay in adjusted multivariate analysis
ascertainment_method: Bayley Scales of Infant Development III at 24 months corrected age
rob_tool: not applied (prospective cohort; no formal RoB tool reported in abstract)
rob_overall: moderate (prospective but non-randomised exposure, single-centre, PN-hyperglycaemia inherently confounded with illness severity)
directness: DIRECT - preterm <32 weeks / <1500g - relevant to Level 3 NICU population
grade_reason: risk of bias (non-randomised exposure to hyperglycaemia, confounding by indication for higher PN intake); single-centre imprecision (n=108)
key_limitation: one of the clearest preterm-specific PN-related hyperglycaemia and ND-outcome studies; motor-delay effect survived adjustment, cognitive delay finding did not have adjusted result reported in abstract
notes: PN-related hyperglycaemia specifically implicated, distinct from stress/illness-related hyperglycaemia mechanism
glucose_threshold_used: >180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) in first week of life
glucose_measurement_method: not specified in abstract (clinical glucose monitoring)
dose_response_reported: N (single threshold/exposure category, not graded dose-response)

design: systematic review and meta-analysis, PROSPERO CRD42022368870
n_patients: 12 studies included (807 infants for hyperglycaemia analysis; 685 for hypoglycaemia analysis)
n_events: death or neurodisability events per pooled analysis
population_detail: infants with neonatal encephalopathy (NE) - DISTINCT population from primary/isolated neonatal hyperglycaemia
intervention: exposure to hyperglycaemia (or hypoglycaemia) in the context of NE
comparator: no exposure to hyperglycaemia (or hypoglycaemia) in the context of NE
outcomes_measured: death or neurodevelopmental impairment at >=18 months
primary_result: hyperglycaemia in NE associated with higher odds of death/neurodisability; hypoglycaemia in NE also associated with higher odds
effect_size: hyperglycaemia: 46.1% vs 28.0%, OR 3.07; hypoglycaemia: 40.6% vs 25.4%, OR 2.17
secondary_results: findings confirmed in subgroup analysis restricted to infants who underwent therapeutic hypothermia
ascertainment_method: ROBINS-I risk of bias assessment; GRADE certainty rating per included study; RevMan inverse-variance fixed-effects meta-analysis
directness: INDIRECT for primary/isolated neonatal hyperglycaemia - this is a NE population where hyperglycaemia is a secondary/stress phenomenon, not primary metabolic dysregulation; flag this distinction explicitly
grade_certainty: Low-Moderate (per GRADE applied within the review to observational studies)
grade_reason: risk of bias (observational studies, ROBINS-I moderate-serious); indirectness (NE population, not isolated hyperglycaemia)
key_limitation: the largest pooled effect size for hyperglycaemia and adverse outcome in this domain, but population is NE-with-secondary-hyperglycaemia, not primary/isolated preterm or term hyperglycaemia - must not be conflated with Zamir/Boscarino's primary-hyperglycaemia populations
notes: PROSPERO CRD42022368870; distinct population flagged per task instructions - a key example of the directness distinction this domain must maintain
gestational_age_range: not specified as single range in abstract (NE population - term/near-term predominant per typical NE case-mix, not preterm-specific)
glucose_threshold_used: not specified as single value in abstract (varies by included study)
glucose_measurement_method: varies by included study (mixed point-of-care/laboratory across pooled studies)
dose_response_reported: N (pooled OR only, not a dose-response gradient)

setting: Leiden University Medical Center, tertiary neonatal centre
design: retrospective follow-up cohort with matched controls
n_patients: 859 infants <=32 weeks screened; 33 hyperglycaemia survivors + 63 matched controls assessed at 2 years
population_detail: infants <=32 weeks gestation admitted to a tertiary neonatal centre 2002-2006
intervention: neonatal hyperglycaemia (blood glucose >=10 mmol/L) treated with insulin for >=12 hours
outcomes_measured: growth (weight/length/head circumference) and neurological/behavioural development at 2 years corrected age
primary_result: growth was similar between groups; neurological and behavioural development were more frequently abnormal in the hyperglycaemia group
effect_size: neurological development abnormal more frequently in hyperglycaemia group; behavioural development abnormal more frequently in hyperglycaemia group
secondary_results: mortality substantially higher in hyperglycaemia group during admission (41% vs 8%, p<0.001), especially in <=1000g or 24-28 week infants
ascertainment_method: retrospective case-note review; standardised neurodevelopmental/behavioural assessment at 2 years corrected age
rob_tool: not applied (retrospective cohort; no formal RoB tool reported in abstract)
rob_overall: moderate-high (retrospective, insulin-treated hyperglycaemia inherently selects for the most unwell survivors - survivor bias likely)
directness: DIRECT - very preterm <=32 weeks, insulin-treated hyperglycaemia population
grade_reason: risk of bias (retrospective, small matched-control comparison, high mortality in exposed group raising survivor-bias concern); imprecision (n=33 exposed survivors)
key_limitation: one of the few studies with a clear insulin-treated preterm hyperglycaemia population and 2-year neurodevelopmental/behavioural outcome; high in-hospital mortality (41%) in the hyperglycaemia group is itself a major finding, separate from the survivor neurodevelopmental signal
notes: PMC2915976 (open access); mortality difference is a critical companion finding to the neurodevelopmental signal in survivors
glucose_threshold_used: >=10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) treated with insulin >=12 hours
glucose_measurement_method: not specified in abstract (clinical blood glucose monitoring)

population_detail: very-low-birth-weight infants (birth weight <1500g), days 1-7 of life
intervention: continuous insulin infusion 0.05 U/kg/h with 20% dextrose support (days 1-7)
outcomes_measured: mortality at expected date of delivery (primary); hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia rates; growth; morbidity
primary_result: no difference in intention-to-treat primary outcome (mortality at EDD) or secondary morbidity; early insulin reduced hyperglycaemia but increased hypoglycaemia; mortality at 28 days was HIGHER in early-insulin group
effect_size: mean glucose 6.2 vs 6.7 mmol/L; hyperglycaemia >10% of week1 in 21% vs 33%; hypoglycaemia (<2.6mmol/L >1h) 29% vs 17%; 28-day mortality higher in insulin group
secondary_results: trial STOPPED EARLY for futility on primary outcome and concern about potential harm; early-insulin group had more carbohydrate infused and less weight loss in week 1 (both statistically significant) - the only clearly favourable secondary signals
ascertainment_method: continuous glucose monitoring used to assess efficacy of glucose control; trial registered ISRCTN78428828
rob_tool: not applied (RCT; early stopping and harm signal noted directly in abstract)
rob_overall: Low (adequately randomised and multicentre, but stopped early with a mortality signal - genuine risk of bias from early stopping plus imprecision from reduced sample)
directness: DIRECT - VLBW/preterm infants - the key interventional (insulin) trial for this population; NO published long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up of this cohort was located this session (see search log)
grade_reason: risk of bias (trial stopped early for futility/harm - a classic source of overestimated harm and underestimated benefit); imprecision (reduced sample from early stopping)
key_limitation: THIS IS THE TRIAL THE RESEARCH BRIEF REFERS TO AS THE 'COIN TRIAL' - no trial by that name exists in the literature (confirmed by targeted search); NIRTURE is the correct identifier. Early insulin REDUCES hyperglycaemia but at the cost of MORE hypoglycaemia and a signal toward HIGHER 28-day mortality - a genuine harm signal, reported with full prominence, not softened. No neurodevelopmental follow-up of this RCT cohort has been published to date - a real evidence gap, not an extrapolation.
notes: Trial stopped early for futility/harm concerns; ISRCTN78428828; this is the single most important interventional trial in this domain and the clearest example of a null/harmful finding given equal prominence to positive findings elsewhere in the domain
glucose_threshold_used: treatment threshold not a single value - insulin titrated to target euglycaemia; hyperglycaemia defined as blood glucose above normal range per protocol
glucose_measurement_method: continuous glucose monitoring used for efficacy assessment; standard glucometer for clinical management
outcome_timepoint: 28 days (mortality only) - NO neurodevelopmental follow-up published
dose_response_reported: N (single intervention arm comparison; no dose-response reported)

n_events: 4 glycaemic groups: normoglycaemic, hypoglycaemic, hyperglycaemic, unstable
population_detail: very preterm infants, birth weight <1500g or gestation <30 weeks, admitted within 24h to a single NZ tertiary unit
intervention: n/a (observational glycaemic-group exposure based on first-week glucose profile)
outcomes_measured: survival without neonatal morbidity; survival without neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years; glucose variability (SD of log-transformed glucose) as a separate predictor
primary_result: hyperglycaemic and unstable groups less likely to survive without morbidity or without neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years IN UNADJUSTED ANALYSIS; NO associations survived adjustment for gestation/birth-weight z-score/socioeconomic status
effect_size: higher mean glucose associated with worse neonatal and 2-year outcomes (unadjusted); greater glucose variability associated with worse neonatal illness but NOT with 2-year outcome
p_value: not reported as single value (multivariable regression reported as non-significant after adjustment)
secondary_results: hypoglycaemic infants had outcomes similar to normoglycaemic infants (null); glucose variability specifically was NOT an independent predictor of 2-year outcome once gestation/birth-weight/SES were accounted for - directly addresses the glycaemic-lability-for-hyperglycaemia question with a NULL result after adjustment
ascertainment_method: retrospective glucose concentration records from first week of life; standardised 2-year neurodevelopmental assessment
rob_tool: not applied (retrospective cohort; no formal RoB tool reported in abstract)
rob_overall: moderate (retrospective, single-centre, but multivariable adjustment for key confounders explicitly performed and changes the headline result)
grade_reason: indirectness/confounding (key finding is that unadjusted glycaemic-group associations do not survive adjustment for gestation and growth - i.e. glycaemia is likely a MARKER of immaturity/growth restriction rather than an independent causal exposure); single-centre imprecision
key_limitation: CENTRAL paper for the glycaemic-variability-in-hyperglycaemia question posed by the task: variability (MAGE/SD-based) was associated with worse NEONATAL illness but NOT independently with 2-year outcome after adjustment - this is a genuine null for variability-as-independent-predictor and should not be overstated as confirming lability's importance
notes: Auckland/Liggins-programme-adjacent (Harding senior author) but methodologically distinct from CHYLD - a retrospective glycaemic-profile cohort, not a treat-to-threshold RCT
gestational_age_range: <30 weeks gestation or <1500g birth weight (very preterm/VLBW)
glucose_threshold_used: exposure defined by profile group, not single threshold; hyperglycaemic/unstable groups defined by absolute glycaemic excursions in first week
glucose_measurement_method: not specified in abstract (retrospective clinical glucose records)
dose_response_reported: Y (variability explicitly tested as a distinct dose-response-style predictor, found non-significant after adjustment)

population_detail: preterm infants randomised within 6 hours of life
intervention: real-time continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)-guided glycaemic management
comparator: blinded CGM with standard intermittent blood glucose-guided management
outcomes_measured: frequency/duration of hypoglycaemic (<47mg/dL) and hyperglycaemic (>180mg/dL) episodes; neurodevelopment at 2 years corrected age via Griffiths Scales
primary_result: CGM significantly reduced both hypoglycaemic and hyperglycaemic episode counts; NO significant difference in neurodevelopmental outcome at 2 years
effect_size: hyperglycaemia episodes first week 145 vs 830; hypoglycaemia episodes first week 339 vs 934; hyperglycaemia at 32 weeks PMA 1 vs 38
secondary_results: reduction in glycaemic excursions did not translate into a detectable neurodevelopmental benefit at 2 years - reported as a null result with equal prominence to the positive glycaemic-control finding
ascertainment_method: real-time CGM device data; Griffiths Scales of Child Development at 2 years corrected age
rob_tool: not applied (RCT; small single-centre trial, no formal RoB tool reported in abstract)
rob_overall: moderate (randomised, single-centre, small sample size likely underpowered for the neurodevelopmental secondary outcome)
grade_reason: imprecision (n=53, and neurodevelopmental outcome was likely underpowered even though glycaemic-episode outcomes were highly significant); single-centre
key_limitation: directly tests whether REDUCING glycaemic variability/excursions (both hypo- and hyperglycaemic) improves neurodevelopmental outcome - answer in this small trial is NO; this is the most direct available test of the 'lability matters more than threshold' hypothesis for hyperglycaemia and it did not confirm a neurodevelopmental benefit from tighter control
notes: Very recent (2026); small trial, likely underpowered for the neurodevelopmental outcome despite being adequately powered for the glycaemic-control primary outcome - flag this distinction clearly
gestational_age_range: not specified as single range in abstract (preterm, randomised within 6h of life)
glucose_threshold_used: hypoglycaemia <47 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L); hyperglycaemia >180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L)
glucose_measurement_method: continuous glucose monitoring (intervention arm) vs intermittent blood glucose (control arm)
dose_response_reported: N (episode counts reported, not a graded dose-response against outcome)
